paras: The killing of Sam Moore took place near Gadsden, Alabama, on December 9, 1888, when deputy sheriffs searching for Moore, a Black man accused of killing a man the night before, found and killed him. The deputies had been shot and wounded by unknown attackers during the search, and they jailed a second man, Lawson Adams, as Moore's supposed accomplice. Papers across the country carried the story chiefly as a forecast that Adams would be lynched.

According to a special dispatch to the Chattanooga Times, Moore, described as 'a negro', was accused of having killed a man on Saturday night, December 8. The dispatch did not name the man he was said to have killed.

On the morning of December 9, Deputy Sheriffs A. C. Christian and A. L. Herzberg went out to 'the new furnace' to arrest Moore, but he had fled. While there, the two deputies 'were shot by unknown parties and wounded.' The wounded officers then went after Lawson Adams, 'supposed to be an accomplice of Moore,' and arrested him and locked him up in jail.

Moore was afterward found and, in the dispatch's words, 'killed for resisting arrest.' The text does not say who fired or describe the encounter, and this version of his death comes only from the officers' side.

The dispatch closed with the expectation that Adams would be 'lynched before morning.' A one-line item in the Sacramento Record-Union the next day reported that a mob at Gadsden threatened to lynch him. No report of Adams's fate, of an inquest into Moore's death, or of the men who shot the deputies appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers through a single wire text, first datelined Chattanooga on December 9 and printed on December 10 in Sacramento, Los Angeles, Savannah and St. Paul. Headline writers fixed on the expected lynching rather than on Moore's death: the Savannah Morning News ran it as 'Lynching Looked For', the Los Angeles Herald as 'More Lynching in Prospect', and the St. Paul Globe as 'Lynching Probable.' The Sacramento Record-Union instead placed it under 'Southern Lawlessness', with a subhead on officers shot while on duty.

A Gadsden-datelined version circulated in weeklies in Ohio and Kentucky from December 13 to 15 under the headline 'Murderer Killed by Officers', which treated the accusation against Moore as established. Shorter versions ran in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, which called Moore 'a negro murderer', and in the Salt Lake Herald's 'Criminal Calendar'. The Somerset Herald in Pennsylvania printed a variant that named the jailed man 'Tom Adams' and left out Moore's killing altogether. No Alabama paper's account was found, and none of the papers questioned the officers' version.

framing.detail: Papers ran the dispatch without comment under headlines that called Moore a 'Negro Murderer' and forecast a lynching ('Lynching Looked For', 'More Lynching in Prospect').
The Sacramento Record-Union grouped it under 'Southern Lawlessness', stressing the shooting of officers.
A Gadsden-datelined version ran in Ohio and Kentucky weeklies as 'Murderer Killed by Officers', treating the accusation as fact.
